lesson.title: Splitting Water: Where Photosynthesis Gets Its Electrons (and Our Oxygen)
lesson.summary: Photolysis is the light driven splitting of water at Photosystem II that replaces electrons lost during the light reactions and releases the oxygen gas that sustains aerobic life.
lesson.body:
Every electron that Photosystem II passes into the electron transport chain has to be replaced from somewhere, or the reaction center would quickly run out of electrons and stop working. Plants solve this by pulling replacement electrons from one of the most abundant and stable molecules available: water. Splitting water to extract electrons, protons, and oxygen is called photolysis, and it is one of the more remarkable feats of biological chemistry, because water's covalent bonds are ordinarily quite difficult to break.

That difficulty connects directly to what makes water water in the first place: its oxygen atom holds electrons more strongly than its hydrogen atoms do, creating polar covalent bonds and an overall bent, polar molecule. Those same strong, polar covalent bonds that make water such an effective solvent and give it its characteristic properties also make it fairly resistant to being pulled apart. Breaking water into its components takes a substantial energy input, and inside the chloroplast, that energy comes directly from light, funneled through the oxidized, electron hungry P680 reaction center of Photosystem II.

The actual chemistry happens at a specialized cluster of manganese and calcium ions bound to Photosystem II, called the oxygen evolving complex. Once P680 loses an electron to the primary acceptor and becomes strongly oxidizing, the oxygen evolving complex pulls one electron at a time from two water molecules, cycling through a series of increasingly oxidized states as it accumulates enough oxidizing power to finally cleave both water molecules at once. The overall reaction converts two water molecules into one oxygen molecule, four protons, and four electrons, with the electrons replenishing Photosystem II's reaction center one at a time as they become available.

The four protons released by this reaction are deposited directly into the thylakoid lumen, adding to the proton gradient that the electron transport chain is simultaneously building through the cytochrome b6f complex, which means water splitting contributes directly to the ATP producing machinery covered in the next concept, not just to electron supply. The oxygen produced, meanwhile, is simply released as a byproduct and diffuses out of the leaf through stomata; the plant has no further chemical use for it. Scientists confirmed this using isotope labeling experiments that tracked oxygen atoms from water into the released gas, settling a long standing question about whether photosynthetic oxygen came from water or from carbon dioxide.

This is worth pausing on: virtually all of the oxygen gas in Earth's atmosphere exists because countless chloroplasts, over billions of years, have been tearing water molecules apart to keep their reaction centers supplied with electrons. Photolysis is not an incidental side reaction, it is the electron source that makes the entire light dependent process possible, and the oxygen we breathe is its byproduct.
